attribution.note: Marcus's own words, labelled by him as his prediction.

semantics.note: Keeps the antecedent (truly mindblowing GPT-5 in 2024) and both consequents (more hype, no burst soon). 'Will' and 'won't' make it firm, so it is a scored conditional.

contract.note: Reading the antecedent as the named GPT-5 released in 2024 is the ordinary reading. A looser 'GPT-5-level advance' reading would still have no capability threshold, so neither reading makes the claim scorable.

evidence.note: OpenAI's own release page dates GPT-5 to Aug 7, 2025. That is reliable for the release date and shows the 2024 antecedent was not met. It is evidence about the condition, not the outcome, so it does not contradict the forecast.

reviews.rationale: The antecedent window closed on 2024-12-31 with no GPT-5 release; GPT-5 came out in August 2025. Because the condition did not happen, the conditional forecast is not scored, as both policy and the contract require.

attribution.note: The assessment that Hoffman's predictions had not borne out is Marcus's own. Hoffman's words are only the object of the claim.

semantics.note: Faithful observation as of the post date, with 'thus far' kept. 'These' predictions is plural and only partly identified.

contract.note: Taking the human-expert hallucination-rate prediction as the referent fits the paragraph that follows. Requiring a matched comparison with experts is strict but defensible. The result depends on that measurement standard.

evidence.note: Identifies Hoffman's prediction of human-expert hallucination rates within months. It says nothing about whether this happened.
A contemporaneous study finds hallucinations in most outputs, which is suggestive. It has no human-expert baseline, so it does not settle parity.

reviews.rationale: The packet identifies the prediction and shows hallucinations were common in early 2024. It contains no matched comparison with human experts, which the contract requires to decide whether the milestone had been reached by March 31, 2024.

attribution.note: Marcus's own statement in his post.

semantics.note: Faithfully gives both parts: size raises cost, and current models are expensive and not reliable enough for many jobs.

contract.note: The plain readings (cost rises with size for comparable architectures; 'many jobs' means several consequential task classes) are ordinary and not stretched either way.

evidence.note: A Feb 2024 technical survey says large parameter counts make training and inference inefficient. It also notes the MoE caveat.
A Jan 2024 study finds legal hallucinations are highly prevalent and warns against unsupervised use in legal tasks.
A Mar 2024 peer-reviewed study finds weaknesses in clinical decision support, so this is a second task class.
Mixtral's active versus total parameters qualify the size-cost link but do not reverse it for comparable models.

reviews.rationale: Contemporaneous technical evidence supports the general size-cost relationship and substantial resource demands; the MoE caveat qualifies it without overturning it. Legal and clinical evaluations show reliability limits across several task classes in early 2024.

attribution.note: Marcus's own statement in his post.

semantics.note: Faithful. 'Most uses' has no stated denominator.

contract.note: Reading 'uses' as enterprise applications fits the surrounding text. Because the speaker named no denominator (projects, organizations or requests), the result depends on which one is chosen.

evidence.note: The Sept 2023 survey covers generative AI broadly at respondent level: most were at early stages and 18% had production apps. Its period and denominator differ from the claim.
Klarna's own announcement of one large live deployment. It cannot establish an industry-wide share.

reviews.rationale: The O'Reilly survey points to mostly early-stage work, but it is from Sept 2023, counts respondents rather than LLM projects, and covers generative AI broadly. Klarna is a single deployment. Nothing in the packet gives the project-level share through March 2024.
